intro: The Zanzibar Archipelago is a group of islands off Tanzania's coast in the Indian Ocean, dominated by Unguja (Zanzibar Island) and Pemba Island. Zanzibar combines one of the Indian Ocean's most beautiful coastlines — white sand beaches, turquoise lagoons, and coral reefs — with a deeply layered history of Arab, Persian, Indian, and Swahili culture visible in Stone Town's UNESCO-listed architecture.

sections.heading: Stone Town — UNESCO World Heritage
sections.content: Stone Town is the living historic heart of Zanzibar, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000. Its narrow coral-stone alleys, ornately carved hardwood doors, and mix of Arab, Indian, and colonial architecture reflect centuries as the Indian Ocean's most important trading port. The Old Fort, House of Wonders, former slave market and Anglican Cathedral, Forodhani Gardens night market, and the Darajani fish auction are all within walking distance. Budget a full day minimum and hire a local guide to unlock the stories behind the facades.

sections.heading: Beaches and Water Activities
sections.content: Zanzibar's north coast (Nungwi, Kendwa) has the calmest swimming conditions year-round, unaffected by tidal variation. The east coast (Paje, Bwejuu, Jambiani) has stronger Indian Ocean winds, making it East Africa's kite-surfing capital. Mnemba Atoll — 30 minutes offshore by boat — is one of the western Indian Ocean's premier dive sites with hawksbill turtles, whale sharks (October–March), and pristine coral gardens. The dolphins at Kizimkazi on the southwest coast are resident year-round; morning snorkel trips allow in-water encounters.

sections.heading: Spice Heritage
sections.content: Zanzibar was the world's largest clove producer throughout the 19th century. The island still grows cloves, cinnamon, cardamom, vanilla, nutmeg, black pepper, and turmeric across interior farms. Half-day spice tours from Stone Town visit working farms, taste raw spices directly from trees and soil, and typically include a Swahili lunch. The spice trade shaped Zanzibar's entire history — the Arab Sultanate of Oman relocated its capital to Stone Town in 1840 specifically to control the clove economy.

sections.heading: Getting There and Around
sections.content: Fast ferries from Dar es Salaam run multiple times daily (75–90 minutes, $35–45 for tourists). Flights are 20 minutes from Dar or 30 minutes from Kilimanjaro Airport. Within Zanzibar, shared dalla-dallas connect Stone Town to beach villages for $0.50–2. Private transfers to Nungwi cost $30–35 one way. Scooter rental ($20/day) is the most flexible option for the interior spice farms and less-visited villages. Taxis are available but negotiate prices before boarding.

faqs.q: How many days should I spend in Zanzibar?
faqs.a: A minimum of 4 days is recommended: 1–2 days in Stone Town, 2–3 days on the beach. 7 days allows a proper combination of cultural exploration, beach relaxation, diving or snorkelling, a spice farm tour, and a dolphin trip without feeling rushed.

faqs.q: What is the best beach in Zanzibar?
faqs.a: Nungwi for calm swimming year-round. Kendwa for the social atmosphere. Paje for kite-surfing. Matemwe for snorkelling and quiet atmosphere. Nungwi is the most popular overall due to tide-free swimming.

Yes — Zanzibar is one of East Africa's best diving destinations. Mnemba Atoll offers pristine coral, sharks, rays, and turtles in 10–30 metres of clear water. Visibility averages 20–30 metres in the dry season. The best diving is June–October.

faqs.q: Do I need a visa for Zanzibar?
faqs.a: Zanzibar is part of Tanzania — your standard Tanzanian tourist visa ($50, on arrival or e-visa) covers both the mainland and the islands. East African Community nationals do not need a visa.

tips: Dress modestly in Stone Town — cover shoulders and knees as it is a predominantly Muslim community
Book Mnemba Atoll dives through a PADI-certified operator for the best experience
The Forodhani night market is best visited early (18:00) before the most popular dishes sell out
Check tide times on the east coast before planning a swim — low tide exposes 500 metres of sand flats
Combine Zanzibar with a Kilimanjaro climb or Northern Circuit safari for the ultimate Tanzania itinerary
